pathway.title: Acadia Healthcare Company, Inc. — Full credit assessment
pathway.question: Should we own this issuer, in which instrument, and why?

runs.text: Leverage is the weakest dimension and the earnings base is clouded. Reported EBITDA is negative for 2025 and the last twelve months after USD 1.01 billion of non-cash impairment, so the usable measure is house-normalised: net debt was 3.01x EBITDA at the end of 2024, 5.72x at the end of 2025 and 4.96x at 2026-09-30. The covenant measure is not available, so no headroom is inferred, and the ratio is high enough that an earnings miss would reach refinancing terms before it reached liquidity. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation N3; calculation C4; 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 88

Free cash flow is thin and rests on one lever, capital spending. Free cash flow was positive at USD 155.62 million in the nine months of 2026 against an outflow of USD 260.43 million a year earlier, but it is still an outflow of USD 23.86 million over the last twelve months, because 2025 capital spending of USD 571.81 million was cut to 6.40% of revenue from 17.26%. Operating cash flow carries little spare capacity if spending resumes. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation N4; calculation N5; calculation N6; calculation N7

Liquidity is adequate for scheduled debt service but is exposed to non-debt claims. Cash plus the undrawn revolver was USD 873.41 million, covering principal due through 2028 1.63 times, while standby letters of credit rose to USD 15.9 million from USD 1.2 million and settlements, uninsured verdicts and a USD 400.0 million past payment show how fast litigation can draw cash; house-normalised EBITDA covered interest expense 2.91x over the last twelve months. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation N2; calculation C1; calculation C3

Refinancing risk is concentrated in three years. Principal due is USD 494.73 million in 2028, USD 536.10 million in 2029 and USD 745.05 million in 2030, which is 75.04% of the total, with the revolver and term-loan balance falling due together in 2030; the notes are fixed rate and the 2025 refinancing removed any earlier bullet, but market access cannot be judged because no prices or ratings were supplied. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation N8; calculation N9; calculation N10; calculation C2

Business quality is strong on scale and diversification and weak on payor mix. The company operates facilities in 40 states and Puerto Rico, no facility is above 4% of revenue and no state above 14%, and 91% of beds outside treatment centers are in owned property excluded from the credit facility pledge, yet Medicaid supplied 61.8% of nine-month 2026 revenue, so federal and state funding decisions set the revenue base. Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 10

Event risk is the main source of downside and part of it is uninsured. A federal criminal investigation and SEC subpoenas cover the acute care line, which was 57.53% of nine-month 2026 revenue, the company has settled matters at USD 400.0 million and USD 179.0 million, and a USD 35.0 million compensatory and USD 70.0 million punitive jury award against an indirect subsidiary is contested. Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 18; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 20

Financial policy is neutral to supportive for creditors. No dividend has ever been paid, repurchases have stopped with USD 250.0 million of authority unused, and debt fell USD 147.61 million in 2026, but the unused authority and equity-linked pay for the chief executive leave restart as a monitoring point. Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation N11

runs.text: Scale, diversification and owned real estate are the main strengths. The company operates 280 facilities with no facility above 4% of revenue and no state above 14%, and 91% of beds outside treatment centers are owned property excluded from the facility pledge; this spreads facility and state risk and gives lenders an unencumbered asset pool, which supports recovery relevance and refinancing confidence. Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 9; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 21

Falling capital intensity and a repaid revolver are the second strength. Capital spending fell to 6.40% of revenue in the nine months of 2026 from 17.26% in 2025 and debt fell by USD 147.61 million in 2026, which turned nine-month free cash flow positive and eased house-normalised net leverage from 5.72x to 4.96x. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation N11

Creditor-neutral financial policy is the third strength. No dividend has ever been paid and repurchases stopped, so no value is extracted from creditors, although the unused authority remains. Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 79; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 54

High leverage on a house-normalised basis is the main weakness. Reported EBITDA is negative for 2025 and the last twelve months after a non-cash impairment, and house-normalised net leverage of 4.96x leaves little room for an earnings miss before refinancing. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C4

Medicaid dependence is the second weakness. Medicaid supplied 61.8% of nine-month 2026 revenue and federal changes cap state directed payments from 2028, so rate cuts would reach a labor-heavy cost base. Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 36–37

Legal and regulatory event risk is the third weakness. The criminal investigation of the acute care line, a contested jury award and insurance exhaustion for some years can turn into cash calls ahead of debt reduction. Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 18; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 20

A concentrated refinancing wall is the fourth weakness. About three-quarters of principal falls due in 2028 to 2030, so market access at that time decides refinancing capacity. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C2

runs.text: No sponsor, buy-out or merger transaction appears in the filings. The financing events are the February 2025 replacement of the credit facility with a USD 1.0 billion revolver and a USD 650.0 million term loan maturing in 2030, and the March 2025 issue of USD 550.0 million of 7.375% senior notes due 2033, whose proceeds repaid revolver borrowings. Growth transactions are small: one acquisition of a 76-bed provider in February 2024 and five joint venture facilities opened in 2025. Excluding impairment, legal settlements, debt extinguishment and property sale results, net debt was 3.01x EBITDA at the end of 2024, 5.72x at the end of 2025 and 4.96x at 2026-09-30, with gross debt at 5.33x.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Business, ownership and governance facts for Acadia Healthcare Company, Inc. (issuer achc-1520697), as of 2026-11-18, on the credit snapshot pathway. The scope is the company's business, structure, ownership, operating model, capital allocation and governance behaviour as stated in the five supplied filings.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Acadia has no sponsor in the filings, so creditor risk comes from payor concentration and legal exposure, not owner extraction: Medicaid supplied 61.8% of revenue in nine months 2026 and a federal criminal investigation of the acute care line is open.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: No dividend has ever been paid and share repurchases stopped at USD 50.4 million in 2025, but 2025 capital spending was debt-funded and the chief executive and chief financial officer changed in 2026. Governance risk is assessed as Medium because the evidence is mixed and the proxy statement with board and holder detail was not supplied.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The filings identify no controlling holder or sponsor, so creditors face no owner-extraction mechanism but also no sponsor equity to cure a shortfall. The company is a NASDAQ-listed holding company, the only investor named is Waud Capital Partners and it appears only in a charter clause that exempts it and its funds from the business-combination limit, with no stake stated, and the holder list sits in a proxy statement that was not supplied.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Payor concentration is the dominant operating risk and it is rising. Medicaid was 57.7% of 2025 revenue and 61.8% of the first nine months of 2026, up from 53.9% in 2023, and Medicare and Medicaid together were about 72% of 2025 revenue. The federal 2025 budget act cuts Medicaid spending, bars new provider taxes and caps state directed payments, with grandfathered programs stepping down by ten percentage points a year from 2028; the company expects little near-term effect from the work requirements because of exemptions, but the payment caps would reduce the rate base behind its largest payor.

fields.name: Quote

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Legal and regulatory exposure is the main event risk and it sits on the largest line. A federal grand jury investigation and SEC subpoenas concern the acute care line, which was 55% of 2025 revenue and 57.53% of nine-month 2026 revenue, covering admissions, length of stay and billing; the company reports no findings and cannot estimate a liability. Settled matters show the cash scale: USD 400.0 million for Desert Hills, USD 179.0 million for the 2019 securities class action with USD 31.5 million insured, and a 2026 jury award of USD 35.0 million compensatory and USD 70.0 million punitive damages against an indirect subsidiary that the subsidiary is contesting.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Insurance does not absorb all of this, which turns verdicts into cash calls. Coverage for the relevant policy year was exhausted by prior losses for the sixth Desert Hills lawsuit and for the excess portion of the Sandoval settlement, and the self-insured professional and general liability reserve rose to USD 214.7 million from USD 181.8 million after a USD 28.6 million unfavourable adjustment in the second quarter of 2026.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Leadership is in transition during the investigations. The chief executive agreement dated 2026-01-19 and the former chief executive's separation dated 2026-01-20 were followed by an interim chief financial officer who signs the second and third-quarter reports, and the returning chief executive holds a one-time option award that vests on share-price hurdles rather than credit measures. Finance continuity is therefore a monitoring point, not a finding of weakness.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Capital allocation has not favoured shareholders at creditors' expense, but growth has been debt-funded. The company has never paid a dividend, used USD 50.4 million of a USD 300.0 million repurchase program in 2025 and none in 2026, leaving USD 250.0 million unused, while 2025 capital spending of USD 571.81 million far exceeded operating cash flow and total debt rose by USD 543.06 million; spending then fell to USD 165.86 million in the nine months of 2026.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Growth is concentrated in acute inpatient care, which is also the line under investigation: acute revenue grew 8.05% in the nine months of 2026 while specialty treatment fell 7.72% and comprehensive treatment centers were flat, so the mix is moving toward the line with the largest regulatory overhang.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The strongest evidence against a Medium rating is that no behaviour in the filings extracts value from creditors: no dividend, a paused repurchase, cut capital spending, USD 147.61 million less debt than at the end of 2025 and no state above 14% of revenue or facility above 4%. The strongest evidence for a higher rating is the open criminal investigation, the rising Medicaid share and uninsured verdicts.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The view would move to Low if the investigations close without charges or a material penalty and Medicaid rate caps are absorbed without margin loss. It would move to High if the investigations produce charges, exclusion risk or a settlement near the scale of the Desert Hills payment, if the contested 2026 jury award is upheld without relief, or if buybacks or debt-funded growth resume while leverage is above its recent range.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Fundamental credit analysis of Acadia Healthcare Company, Inc. (issuer achc-1520697), as of 2026-11-18, on the credit snapshot pathway. The scope is the issuer's business, structure, earnings, cash flow, liquidity, refinancing and downside, synthesised from the five supplied filings and the three earlier analyses.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Acadia is a large, mostly owned behavioral healthcare operator whose credit is constrained by high leverage, near-zero free cash flow and open Medicaid and legal risks, so creditors depend on capital spending staying low and a clean investigation outcome.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Net debt was USD 2.19 billion at 2026-09-30, 4.96x house-normalised EBITDA, because reported EBITDA is negative after a non-cash impairment; liquidity of USD 873.41 million exceeds the USD 535.35 million of principal due through 2028, but the 2028 to 2030 maturities will need refinancing.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Leverage is the weakest dimension and the earnings base is clouded. Reported EBITDA is negative for 2025 and the last twelve months after USD 1.01 billion of non-cash impairment, so the usable measure is house-normalised: net debt was 3.01x EBITDA at the end of 2024, 5.72x at the end of 2025 and 4.96x at 2026-09-30. The covenant measure is not available, so no headroom is inferred, and the ratio is high enough that an earnings miss would reach refinancing terms before it reached liquidity.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Free cash flow is thin and rests on one lever, capital spending. Free cash flow was positive at USD 155.62 million in the nine months of 2026 against an outflow of USD 260.43 million a year earlier, but it is still an outflow of USD 23.86 million over the last twelve months, because 2025 capital spending of USD 571.81 million was cut to 6.40% of revenue from 17.26%. Operating cash flow carries little spare capacity if spending resumes.

fields.value: Liquidity is adequate for scheduled debt service but is exposed to non-debt claims. Cash plus the undrawn revolver was USD 873.41 million, covering principal due through 2028 1.63 times, while standby letters of credit rose to USD 15.9 million from USD 1.2 million and settlements, uninsured verdicts and a USD 400.0 million past payment show how fast litigation can draw cash; house-normalised EBITDA covered interest expense 2.91x over the last twelve months.

fields.value: Refinancing risk is concentrated in three years. Principal due is USD 494.73 million in 2028, USD 536.10 million in 2029 and USD 745.05 million in 2030, which is 75.04% of the total, with the revolver and term-loan balance falling due together in 2030; the notes are fixed rate and the 2025 refinancing removed any earlier bullet, but market access cannot be judged because no prices or ratings were supplied.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Business quality is strong on scale and diversification and weak on payor mix. The company operates facilities in 40 states and Puerto Rico, no facility is above 4% of revenue and no state above 14%, and 91% of beds outside treatment centers are in owned property excluded from the credit facility pledge, yet Medicaid supplied 61.8% of nine-month 2026 revenue, so federal and state funding decisions set the revenue base.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Event risk is the main source of downside and part of it is uninsured. A federal criminal investigation and SEC subpoenas cover the acute care line, which was 57.53% of nine-month 2026 revenue, the company has settled matters at USD 400.0 million and USD 179.0 million, and a USD 35.0 million compensatory and USD 70.0 million punitive jury award against an indirect subsidiary is contested.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Financial policy is neutral to supportive for creditors. No dividend has ever been paid, repurchases have stopped with USD 250.0 million of authority unused, and debt fell USD 147.61 million in 2026, but the unused authority and equity-linked pay for the chief executive leave restart as a monitoring point.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The strongest evidence against a weak view is the direction of travel: house-normalised net leverage fell from 5.72x to 4.96x, free cash flow turned positive at USD 155.62 million in the nine months, debt fell USD 147.61 million and no behaviour in the filings extracts value from creditors. The strongest evidence for a weaker view is that the improvement comes mainly from cutting capital spending, the earnings base used for leverage is a house measure, and legal outcomes are unquantified.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: The view would improve if the investigations close without a material penalty, same-facility growth holds while capital spending stays low for a further year, and the compliance certificate shows covenant room on the agreement's own definition. It would worsen if Medicaid directed-payment caps or eligibility rules reduce revenue per patient day, if an investigation or the contested jury award produces a payment near the scale of the Desert Hills settlement, or if repurchases or growth spending resume before the 2028 notes are refinanced.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Acadia runs 280 behavioral healthcare facilities with about 12,800 beds in 40 states and Puerto Rico through the subsidiaries of a listed holding company. Acute inpatient psychiatric care was 55% of 2025 revenue, specialty treatment 17%, comprehensive treatment centers for opioid use 17% and residential treatment 11%. Demand is clinical and non-discretionary and entry is limited by licensing and certificate-of-need rules, which supports volume visibility, but 72% of revenue comes from Medicare and Medicaid at predetermined rate schedules, so cash-flow visibility rests on government budgets and the company cannot recover cost increases through price.

fields.value: The asset base supports refinancing confidence: 91% of beds outside treatment centers sit in owned property, maintenance capital spending is about 3% of revenue, no facility exceeds 4% of revenue and no state exceeds 14%. These features limit the damage from a single facility or state event but do not offset the payor concentration.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: No sponsor or controlling holder is identified, so there is no extraction vehicle and no equity backstop; the only investor named, Waud Capital Partners, has a charter carve-out and no stated stake. The wholly-owned U.S. subsidiaries guarantee the credit facility and the three note series, while real property is excluded from the facility pledge, and 19 facilities are held through joint ventures in which partners own 5% to 35% and hold put rights on a change of control over USD 229.88 million of redeemable interests that sit outside debt. The risk for creditors is therefore event and payor risk, not owner behaviour, and governance risk is assessed as Medium because of open investigations and leadership turnover.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Revenue is predictable in volume but not in price. Same-facility revenue grew 4.0% in the nine months of 2026, with patient days up 1.2%, admissions up 6.5% and revenue per patient day up 2.8%, so growth is admission and price led while stays shorten. Government payors reimburse on predetermined rate schedules and Medicaid supplied 61.8% of revenue against 53.9% in 2023, which ties pricing power to state budgets and to the federal budget act that caps state directed payments from 2028. Consolidated revenue grew 5.04% in 2025 and 3.96% in the nine months of 2026, and the shift of mix toward acute inpatient care increases dependence on the line under investigation.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Margins have compressed and the cost base is largely fixed. Salaries, wages and benefits were 55.27% of nine-month 2026 revenue, the company reports a shortage of nurses and counselors that forces wage increases and costlier contract labor, and other operating expenses, mainly purchased services, insurance and provider taxes, rose to 16.7% of 2025 revenue from 14.0% and were 16.3% in the nine months of 2026 with a USD 28.6 million unfavourable liability adjustment. House-normalised EBITDA margin fell to 12.48% in 2025 from 19.82% in 2024 and was 12.94% for the last twelve months, so margins cannot be defended under volume pressure without cost action, and cost flexibility sits mainly in growth capital spending rather than operating costs.

fields.value: EBITDA converts to free cash flow only when growth spending is cut. Maintenance capital spending is about 3% of revenue, but total spending was 17.26% of 2025 revenue and 6.40% in the nine months of 2026; operating cash flow of USD 321.48 million in the nine months funded USD 165.86 million of spending and a revolver paydown. Cash paid for interest was USD 124.66 million in 2025 against interest expense, net of USD 138.86 million, government investigation costs fell to USD 38.16 million in the nine months of 2026 from USD 123.27 million, and last-twelve-month interest cover on an accrual basis was 2.91x, so free cash flow after interest remains small.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Rivalry is moderate and local: competitors include non-profit and government-owned providers with tax advantages and independent operators with strong reputations, which can reduce patient volume if they recruit staff or win payor contracts better. Entry is limited by licensing, accreditation and certificate-of-need approval, which protects existing beds. Substitutes matter through lower-cost settings and shorter stays, with same-facility length of stay down 5.0% in the nine months of 2026. Buyer power is high because government programs and managed care set rates, and supplier power sits mainly in scarce nurses, counselors and psychiatrists. Together these forces cap pricing and keep labor cost high, which limits margin durability.

fields.value: Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 16; 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 43; 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 67; 10-K_2025-12-31_achc_achc-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 69; 10-Q_2026-09-30_achc_achc-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 38

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Political and regulatory factors are a primary credit driver. The federal budget act reduces federal Medicaid spending, bars new provider taxes, caps state directed payments and requires work or community engagement rules by 2026-12-31 with six-monthly eligibility checks, and the company also faces criminal and securities investigations; economic factors matter through loss of insurance coverage after the end of enhanced marketplace subsidies. Social and technological factors do not appear to be primary credit drivers on the materials supplied, apart from cybersecurity incidents the company discloses it has experienced.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Strengths are scale across 40 states, owned real estate, no facility above 4% of revenue, falling capital intensity and no extraction by owners. Weaknesses are leverage that is high on a house-normalised basis, negative reported EBITDA, thin free cash flow, a labor-heavy cost base and Medicaid dependence. Opportunities that could improve credit quality are joint venture growth funded by partners, deleveraging from lower spending and closing the investigations. Threats are Medicaid funding changes, penalties or uninsured verdicts, wage inflation and a refinancing wall in 2028 to 2030.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: On a ratings-style lens the financial profile is weak to average. Scale and market position are strong, competitive advantage and business diversification are average because service lines are spread but payors are concentrated, cost and capex flexibility is average because spending can be cut but labor cannot, margin stability and free cash flow stability are weak, the ability to refinance is average with market access not assessable, liquidity is average to strong, and financial policy and governance are average. The main supports are scale, owned real estate, liquidity and deleveraging since 2025; the main constraints are leverage on an unmeasured covenant basis, thin free cash flow and event risk; the trend is improving from the 2025 trough; missing datapoints are covenant earnings, market pricing and investigation outcomes.

The first operational break is revenue per patient day, because government rate schedules do not rise with cost while salaries, wages and benefits are 55.27% of revenue, so margin falls faster than revenue. The financial transmission is lower house-normalised EBITDA against fixed debt, which lifts leverage above the 4.96x reached at 2026-09-30, while a settlement of the scale of the USD 400.0 million paid in 2024 would equal 45.80% of current liquidity of USD 873.41 million. The liquidity consequence is manageable through 2028 because liquidity covers scheduled principal 1.63 times, but the refinancing consequence is severe if leverage is high when the 2028 notes must be refinanced. Management levers are growth capital spending, held-for-sale property, the paused repurchase program and revolver availability; the observable triggers are same-facility revenue per patient day, the Medicaid share of revenue and any investigation development. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on market access that is not assessable here and on leverage at the time the 2028 notes mature. The primary downside path is a Medicaid payment cut combined with a legal cash call while leverage is high. fields.value: Scale, diversification and owned real estate are the main strengths. The company operates 280 facilities with no facility above 4% of revenue and no state above 14%, and 91% of beds outside treatment centers are owned property excluded from the facility pledge; this spreads facility and state risk and gives lenders an unencumbered asset pool, which supports recovery relevance and refinancing confidence.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Falling capital intensity and a repaid revolver are the second strength. Capital spending fell to 6.40% of revenue in the nine months of 2026 from 17.26% in 2025 and debt fell by USD 147.61 million in 2026, which turned nine-month free cash flow positive and eased house-normalised net leverage from 5.72x to 4.96x.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Creditor-neutral financial policy is the third strength. No dividend has ever been paid and repurchases stopped, so no value is extracted from creditors, although the unused authority remains.

fields.value: High leverage on a house-normalised basis is the main weakness. Reported EBITDA is negative for 2025 and the last twelve months after a non-cash impairment, and house-normalised net leverage of 4.96x leaves little room for an earnings miss before refinancing.

fields.value: Medicaid dependence is the second weakness. Medicaid supplied 61.8% of nine-month 2026 revenue and federal changes cap state directed payments from 2028, so rate cuts would reach a labor-heavy cost base.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Legal and regulatory event risk is the third weakness. The criminal investigation of the acute care line, a contested jury award and insurance exhaustion for some years can turn into cash calls ahead of debt reduction.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: A concentrated refinancing wall is the fourth weakness. About three-quarters of principal falls due in 2028 to 2030, so market access at that time decides refinancing capacity.
